title: Basket or oven-style air fryer: what should you compare?
dek: Two shapes, two failure modes. The trade-offs that decide it are on the listing, if you know which fields to read.
author: Crisp Report desk
provenance: Written as a comparison method. No unit on this desk has been cooked in, and no product below is recommended - the five links we were given are still unresolved, so this page deliberately names nothing.

blocks.x: The choice between a basket drawer and an oven-style unit is not about which cooks better. It is about which inconvenience you would rather live with: shaking and refilling a drawer in batches, or dedicating a permanent slice of counter to a box with a door. Both are workable. Both get returned for the wrong reason.
Start with the shape of what you actually cook

Write down three things you would realistically make in it twice a month. Not the aspirational list - the ordinary one. Then look at each item's geometry: a tray of wings lies flat, a whole small chicken does not; frozen fries want a wide, shallow layer, roasted chickpeas want air on all sides and tolerate a deeper pile.

A single-layer basket is the honest answer for anything you want crisped on two faces, because nothing sits on top of it. An oven-style unit with two racks and a rotisserie is the honest answer for volume in one go, because it trades contact with the surface for a second level. If your three items all lie flat, the second set of features is money spent on a mode you will not use.
Before you compare any two models, answer these three:
items: Do I need to cook **one big flat layer** or **two stacked smaller ones**?
Will food need turning halfway - and do I have a reason to care (yes for crisped surfaces, no for a casserole dish)?
Does anything I cook need a **rotating spit**, or a **vertical clearance** taller than the drawer can give? Those two requirements eliminate most drawers outright, whatever the spec sheet claims.

blocks.x: Six fields on the listing that actually decide it

head: Field
Why it decides the shape
How to check it
rows: Internal chamber dimensions, not stated litres
A volume figure can include the door cavity, the element housing or the rack stack
Compare the length × width × height numbers against one item from your list. If only a litre figure is given, treat the capacity as unverified.
Number of rack or shelf positions
This is the real difference between a drawer and an oven
Count the physical positions in the gallery, not the modes in the marketing copy.
Window and light
Oven styles earn their door; drawer styles rarely need one
If the listing has no window image, assume you will open it to look, which costs heat.
Removable parts list
Drawer = one basket to wash; oven = racks, tray, door glass
Find the parts diagram. Whatever is not shown as removable is what you will be wiping with a cloth.
Power figure
Compare like with like between listings, not against a household guess
Note the wattage each listing states and put the two numbers side by side; a bigger chamber at the same draw behaves differently from a small one.
Clearance stated in the manual
Oven styles usually want more breathing room around the exhaust
The manual is a linked PDF on most listings. Measure the space you have against that figure before the box arrives.
Rotation of the fan housing
Determines whether you can push it near a wall

Photograph the spot you have in mind and note what is beside the exhaust. If the answer is a cabinet side, a wall or a socket, the manual’s clearance figure becomes the deciding number, not the marketing copy.
blocks.caption: Every row is a field you can verify on a listing in about a minute. None of them requires us to have tested a product.

blocks.x: Why this page carries no model names. We were given five links to build this desk around. Each identifier in them measures nine characters, which we cannot resolve to a listing, so no title, price or rating appears anywhere on this site. A guide that named a product today would be naming a guess. The full record is on the Desk page and in Flagged for review.

Drawer units fail in households for a boring reason: the coating on the basket wears, and a replacement is either sold separately or not at all. Oven units fail for an equally boring reason: the door glass, the hinge and the seal are three more things that can be damaged by a scrubber, and they are rarely cheap or quick to replace.

Before you buy, run one search: the brand plus the word for the part you would most plausibly need in year two. If a coating or a gasket is not obtainable, the appliance has a shorter practical life than its warranty suggests, and the shape decision becomes a repairability decision. That is checkable from the listing page and the brand's own support area - not from a review score.
What we cannot tell you, and would rather say so

items: Which of the two shapes cooks more evenly in our kitchen. Nobody here cooked anything.
Whether a specific model is quieter, faster, or better built. Those are listing claims until someone measures them.

Any price, discount or 'best value' judgement. Prices may only be shown by Amazon-served content or an approved API, and we have neither; a comparison table with invented numbers is the fastest way to lose an affiliate account and a reader's trust in one commit.
Any star rating or review count. Amazon's participation requirements tie the display of reviews and ratings to a link obtained through the approved APIs, which we do not have.

blocks.x: Choose the drawer if you cook flat, single-layer food, wash as you go, and store the thing in a cupboard. Choose the oven style if you cook for more than two at once, want two racks or a rotisserie in the same run, and have a permanent stretch of counter that satisfies the clearance the manual asks for on the exhaust side. If both describe you, the tie-breaker is not performance - it is whether you would rather carry one basket to the sink or wipe a door.
